reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Fungal infection of the external auditory canal presenting with intense itching, a feeling of blockage, discharge, and sometimes dull pain and reduced hearing
Aspergillus (often niger) and Candida are the usual organisms, and Aspergillus classically shows blotting-paper or wet newspaper debris with black or fungal spore heads
It is more common in hot humid climates, in swimmers, in diabetics, and after prolonged use of topical antibiotic-steroid ear drops
Diagnosis is largely clinical on otoscopy, supported by microscopy and culture of the debris when the picture is unclear
The mainstay of treatment is thorough and repeated aural toilet to remove fungal debris, followed by topical antifungal agents and keeping the ear dry
Correcting predisposing factors such as excessive moisture, glucose control in diabetics, and stopping unnecessary topical antibiotics is important to prevent recurrence
An intact tympanic membrane should be confirmed, as this influences the choice of topical agent
Recurrence is common if debris is incompletely cleared or predisposing factors persist
reference.pathophysiology: Otomycosis is a superficial fungal infection of the squamous epithelium lining the external auditory canal. A warm, moist, and often macerated canal, frequently after water exposure or suppression of normal flora by topical antibiotics, favours colonisation by saprophytic fungi such as Aspergillus and Candida. The fungi proliferate over the canal skin and cerumen, producing hyphal mats and spores that trigger itching and inflammation. Accumulated debris obstructs the canal and can retain moisture, perpetuating the cycle. In immunocompromised or diabetic patients infection may be more aggressive.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic suppurative otitis media with discharge
Necrotising (malignant) otitis externa in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy to identify characteristic fungal debris and confirm tympanic membrane integrity
Microscopy and fungal culture of canal debris when diagnosis is uncertain or disease is resistant
Blood glucose or diabetic screening in recurrent or severe cases
Consideration of underlying immunosuppression in aggressive or persistent infection
redFlags: Severe deep pain, granulations at the bony-cartilaginous junction, or cranial nerve signs suggesting necrotising otitis externa in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient
Facial weakness or systemic upset indicating spread beyond the canal
Failure to respond to appropriate treatment raising concern for invasive fungal disease
Discharge through a perforation suggesting middle-ear involvement
reference.prognosis: With thorough aural toilet, topical antifungal treatment, and control of predisposing factors the outlook is excellent, though recurrences are frequent when the ear is not kept dry or debris is inadequately cleared; invasive disease is rare and confined largely to immunocompromised hosts.
pitfalls: Prescribing topical antifungals without first removing the fungal debris, which limits their effect
Continuing antibiotic-steroid drops that promoted the fungal overgrowth in the first place
Missing an underlying diabetes or immunosuppression in recurrent disease
Failing to recognise early necrotising otitis externa in an at-risk patient
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Repeated thorough aural toilet under otoscopy or microsuction to remove fungal debris, the mainstay of treatment
Topical antifungal agents such as clotrimazole applied after debris clearance
Keep the ear dry and avoid water exposure to interrupt the moist environment that sustains fungal growth
Stop unnecessary topical antibiotic-corticosteroid drops that suppress normal flora and predispose to fungal overgrowth
Optimise glycaemic control in diabetics and consider underlying immunosuppression in aggressive or persistent disease
Microscopy and culture of debris to guide therapy in resistant cases, with follow-up given the frequent recurrences
